blocks.h: Why split and join instead of finding the k-th space?
p: Finding the position of the k-th space by hand needs a loop and a special case when fewer than k spaces exist. `split()[:k]` clips automatically and `join` rebuilds the text. The cost is a temporary list of all words; an O(1)-extra-space version scans for the k-th space and slices once.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the word list.

1816.takeaway: Split into words, slice the first k, join with spaces.

blocks.h: Why sort once and use a heap?
p: At each decision the candidates are exactly the tasks with enqueueTime ≤ now that haven't run; the heap picks the shortest in O(log n). Sorting by enqueue time lets a single moving pointer add each task to the heap once. Total O(n log n).

blocks.h: Why binary search on the speed?
p: Total time only decreases as the speed grows, so 'feasible' is monotone. Instead of testing every speed, binary search halves the range each time and each test is one O(n) pass. The ceiling division reflects waiting for the next whole hour after each ride except the last.

bullets: Time: O(n log S) where S is the maximum speed (10⁷).

blocks.h: Why binary search on the length?
p: A longer piece length always gives fewer (or equal) pieces, so 'at least k pieces' is true up to some maximum length and false after. That monotone property makes binary search work, with an O(n) check each time.

1891.takeaway: Binary search on the piece length: count pieces with sum(r // length) and keep the largest length that yields at least k.

p: Every substring that ends in an odd digit is odd, and among substrings, the longest one has the most digits and so the largest value (the input has no leading zero problem for the whole prefix). bullets: Space: O(n) for the returned slice.

1903.takeaway: A number is odd by its last digit, so cut the string right after its last odd digit.

blocks.h: Why use the first and last occurrence?
p: A palindrome `c m c` needs a c before m and a c after it. If any pair of c's works, the outermost pair (first and last) works too, because the middle part only grows. So for each c, the set of possible middle letters is exactly the set of letters between the first and last c, and distinct (c, m) pairs are distinct palindromes.

1930.takeaway: For every outer letter take the span between its first and last occurrence; the distinct letters inside are the possible middles.

p: After cancelling matches, the string looks like `]]...][[...[` (k unmatched `]` followed by k unmatched `[`, with k = 3). Swapping the first `[` from the right part with the last `]` from the left part fixes two pairs at once. So k pairs need ceil(k/2) swaps. For k = 3 that is 2: after one swap the string is `[]][][` and a second swap finishes.

1963.takeaway: Cancel matched brackets with a counter; the leftover k unmatched pairs need ceil(k/2) swaps.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Maximum of everything to the left of i
Everything to the left is smaller and everything to the right is larger
Chained comparison; x is where it would be in sorted order
The first element has nothing on its left; the last has nothing on its right

p: If some element to the left is larger than x, a pivot at that element makes the search discard x's side when looking for x ('pivot > target → discard from the pivot on'). Symmetrically, a smaller element to the right can be a pivot that discards x's side. If all left elements are smaller and all right elements are larger, no pivot can ever send the search away from x, so x is always found.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the suffix minimum array.

1966.takeaway: A value is always found iff everything left of it is smaller and everything right of it is larger: prefix maximum and suffix minimum.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The largest number 2^p − 1 (all p bits set)
2^p − 2: all ones except the lowest bit
The partner of 1 in each pair
All numbers except the maximum split into pairs (x, 2^p − 1 − x)
Python's three-argument `pow` runs in O(log e)
Largest number times the pairs' product

p: `p = 3` → 1512: the numbers are 1…7. The best arrangement is `7` plus 3 pairs of `(1, 6)`; product = 7 · 6³ = 1512.

blocks.h: Why does the minimum product look like this?
p: Swapping bits between two numbers keeps their SUM fixed, and for a fixed sum the product of two positive numbers is smallest when they are as far apart as possible: (1, sum−1). Every pair (x, 2^p − 1 − x) has sum 2^p − 1 and can be turned into (1, 2^p − 2) by moving bits. The maximum 2^p − 1 can't be paired, so it stays. The closed form matches an exhaustive search over all bit-swap sequences for p = 1, 2, 3: True.

bullets: Time: O(p) for the modular power.

1969.takeaway: Swaps keep pair sums fixed, so the product is minimised by turning every pair into (1, 2^p − 2) and leaving 2^p − 1 alone.

blocks.h: Why does a plain queue give increasing order?
p: BFS (Breadth-First Search) by length: all 1-digit numbers, then all 2-digit numbers, and so on. Within one length, appending digits in increasing order to numbers popped in increasing order keeps the queue sorted. So the first number meeting the condition is the smallest. p: If `t` repeated k times is a subsequence of s, so is any prefix of `t` repeated k times, so valid strings grow one letter at a time from valid shorter ones. Candidates that fail are never extended. Because only letters occurring at least k times are used and the answer has at most n/k letters, the number of candidates stays small.

bullets: Time: O(n · 26^(n/k)) worst case, but pruning makes it fast in practice.

2014.takeaway: BFS (Breadth-First Search) over strings built from frequent letters, extending only candidates whose k-fold repetition is a subsequence.

p: With p ≠ s, a pair picks one index holding p and a different index holding s, so counts multiply. When p == s (here `'77'` + `'77'`), the same set of indexes serves both roles and `i ≠ j` removes the pairs where both picks are the same index: cnt·cnt − cnt = cnt·(cnt−1).

p: `[3,9,7,3]` (n = 2, total = 22): left half `[3,9]`, right half `[7,3]`. Candidate chosen sums (k from the left, 2−k from the right) and the difference they produce; best = 2:
